What the numbers *do* support is the diagnosis behind it: the arrival cost is
`arrivals ÷ lanes × open cost`, so the levers are the number of lanes (memory) and the
open cost (already halved by the one-flight open, and the rest needs the record layer
that bulk rejected). Neither is pre-warming.

**And the lane count does not move it either, which refutes my own arithmetic
(2026-11-02).** The paragraph above attributes the `churn-16` tail to
`16 × 2.5 ms ÷ 4 lanes`. The bench can set the pool width without a code change, so
that is directly testable — `--arm id=l4,pool_cap=N`, four rounds each:

| lanes | `l4` p99 | its A/A twin | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 18.83 ms | 17.42 ms | 3 793 |
| 8 | 17.06 ms | 19.11 ms | 3 907 |
| 16 | 17.55 ms | 17.45 ms | 4 042 |

**The within-configuration scatter (17.06-19.11) is as large as the whole
between-configuration range (17.1-18.8).** Quadrupling the pool changes nothing. So
the tail is not lane queueing, and the `16 × 2.5 ÷ 4` explanation is **withdrawn** —
it was arithmetic that fitted a number, which is the fifth time this cycle has
recorded that failure mode.

What is left is a precise negative characterisation, and it is worth stating because
it is now narrow: under sixteen concurrent fresh connections the tail is **15-20 ms**
and it is not lanes, not a slow opening (zero past 100 ms on either side), not the
pairing (zero budgets expired), not a multi-second stall (those are fixed), and not
the carrier's timer or window (both measured at parity on `rr-16`). It is a
distributed tail that no single structural lever moves.

The honest reading is that this is the cost of **one handshake per arrival under
concurrency** — the thing TCP does not pay, because it multiplexes — and that the two
levers named two paragraphs ago are the only ones left: the number of lanes (measured,
flat) and the cost of an open (halved once by the one-flight open; the rest needs the
record layer that the bulk cell rejected three times). **P1′'s p99 gate and P2′'s
"level with TCP" gate are therefore open, and they are open because of a structural
choice this release does not reverse**, which is exactly what `CHANGELOG.md`'s Known
gaps says in the release notes.

**P5′: the release ritual, run in order, and held where the gate says (2026-11-02).**
The five steps of `docs/release.md`, with what each produced:

1. **`just interop`** — 3 of 3. `new_server_refuses_old_client_and_keeps_serving`
   passes, so a 1.0.0 client meets a v0.11.2 binary and both refuse each other on the
   connection it happens on while each keeps serving its own version. (This step was
   broken for the whole cycle until `3dc48aa`: the released-side config was still
   written in v0.11.1's schema, so the old server refused its own config before the
   wire was ever tested.)
2. **`just bench peers fetch`** — frp 0.71.1, rathole 0.5.0, nps 0.26.10, from their
   latest GitHub releases, recorded in the results meta.
3. **The sweep** — `just bench --profile sweep --binary target/release/molehill --out
   benches/records/results-bench-v1.0.0.json`, five arms over the staged schedule and
   the capacity ramp, fingerprint `0e549bbb810395a3`, running now.
4. **The charts and the README tables** — cannot be produced from a record whose gate
   fails, and are not produced speculatively.
5. **`just bench gate`** — **the honest blocker.** Run against the timeline alone on
   this tree it reports four of its five axes green (coverage, the endpoint invariant,
   drift, and the regression half correctly reported as absent) and **two named SLO
   failures**: `timeline[clean]` p99 **93.02 ms** and `timeline[clean#2]` p99
   **93.56 ms**, against a 50 ms bar.

So the release is **held at step 5**, on two numbers, and the numbers moved by an order
of magnitude in this cycle (they were 668 and 376 ms). What remains is the same
structural gap the Known gaps entry describes: a fresh connection runs its own
handshake, sixteen concurrent arrivals contend for it, and the tail that produces is
43 ms too long for this SLO. **No tag is pushed, and none will be by me** — the CHANGELOG
section, the version and the ritual are in place so that a human who accepts the gap can
tag, and one who does not has the number to argue with.

**And the sweep found that the two SLO failures were not the only blocker — a
five-stage cascade starts at `loss5` (2026-11-02).** The five-arm sweep's molehill arm
reads:

`clean: 46.248 ms; rtt100: 403.175; loss1: 1101.306; loss5: FAILED; rate100: FAILED;
rate20: FAILED; jitter: FAILED; clean#2: FAILED`, and `capacity: ramp 8`.

**Two landmarks, and they are the first of the cycle:** `clean` at **46.2 ms is inside
the 50 ms SLO** — the arrival fix did that, from 668 ms two runs ago — and
**`capacity` climbed all eight levels**, `capacity_streams = 8` = `streams_max`, where
five rounds in six had never passed level one.

And five stages failed, all with `iperf3 error: control socket has closed
unexpectedly`, cascading from the first. The `loss5` sink's own log says what the
first one was:

`unable to receive cookie at server: Bad file descriptor`, `wall_s 0.85`.

So the `loss5` sample died 0.85 s in, and **every stage after it failed for the same
reason** — AGENTS §10 names this exact hazard ("a wedged iperf3 server turned every
later repetition into a null"), and it is the same signature as the sweep that opened
this cycle, which was attributed to the arrival tail at the time and may not have
been. **A `Bad file descriptor` on the sink's first test is either the product closing
a stream under 5 % loss or the harness's sink lifetime; the two are separable, and
until they are, a single failure costs five stages of evidence.**

Two things follow, and the second one is uncomfortable. The cascade is a harness defect
worth fixing on its own (restart the sink after a failed sample, which §10 requires and
`iperf_sink` does not do mid-stage). And the earlier conclusion that "the arrival gap
fails the release sweep" now has a competing explanation for four of those five
failures — the same cascade — which means **the `clean` and `capacity` numbers above,
not the failure list, are the part of this run to trust**.

**And followed up, the cascade has two shapes and neither is the sink (2026-11-02).**
The `Bad file descriptor` line is **normal** — it appears on every stage's sink at test
#1, and `loss1`, which *passed*, has it too: it is the readiness probe hitting the port
before the sink is listening, and it is not the cause. Counting the sink's accepted
connections per stage gives the real picture:

| stage | sink accepted | reported |
|---|---|---|
| `clean` | 1 | pass, 46.2 ms |
| `loss1` | 1 | pass, 1 101 ms |
| **`loss5`** | **0** | FAILED |
| **`clean#2`** | **1** | FAILED |

So `loss5` never reached the sink at all — the tool did not forward the visitor's
connection — while `clean#2` reached it and then failed mid-test. Two shapes, both
consistent with the tool's **data path being unhealthy after the lossy stages**, and
both *before* `capacity`, which then climbed all eight levels in the same arm. So the
tool recovered between the end of the timeline and the capacity scenario.

**That revises the cycle's opening conclusion for the second time.** The sweep that
started this work failed `loss5`, `rate100`, `jitter` and `clean#2` — the same four
stages — and that was read as "the arrival gap fails the release sweep" and became a
`CHANGELOG` Known gap. It is now at least as likely that the cause is **a post-loss
data-path failure that persists for stages and then clears**, which is a more serious
defect than a latency tail and a completely different one. The honest status of that
Known gap is "the observation is real, the attribution is open", and it should say so
until the two are separated.

Separating them is the next measurement and it is cheap: a **clean-only** schedule
(`--condition clean`) beside one that goes through `loss5`, so the post-loss state is
the only variable. Already ruled out: the sink (fresh per stage), the readiness probe
(`Bad file descriptor` is normal), and the arrival tail (46.2 ms on the clean stage,
inside the SLO).

**And the first hypothesis about it — my own age bound blocking openings — was built,
measured and reverted (2026-11-02).** The reasoning was sound: the write path applies
the age bound *before* the opening exemption, so on a lane whose oldest data packet is
older than the RTO (which is what a 5 % loss path produces) a new stream's handshake
can write nothing at all. That would look exactly like the measured intermittency: the
same binary reading `churn-16` p99 760 ms in one copy and 20.6 ms in its A/A twin under
`--condition loss5`.

Built — openings exempt from the age bound — and measured under the same condition:

| | before | openings exempt |
|---|---|---|
| `churn-16` p50 | 2.63 ms | **202.05** (both arms identical) |
| `churn-16` p99 | 760 ms (twin 20.6) | 861 (both arms identical) |
| `bulk-n` | 6.36 (twin 11.22) | **1.51** (twin 1.42) |

**Worse on every axis, and worse in a more worrying way: the A/A twins now agree
exactly.** Before, the two copies of one binary disagreed by 37× — intermittency.
After, they agree to the hundredth of a millisecond — a uniformly bad deterministic
path. So the exemption did not fix the intermittency; it removed the variance by
making the degradation total. Reverted.

Two things are established and one is not. The exemption is wrong in this form (it lets
every new stream past a bound whose whole purpose is to keep the flight young, and the
bulk cell pays 4× for it). The intermittency under 5 % loss is real — 760 against 20.6
in one run of one binary — and it is now the last unexplained thing in the release
picture. What is **not** established is that the age bound causes it: the exemption
changed the symptoms without removing them, which is evidence against that reading.

The next measurement should therefore be the one that does not presuppose a cause: run
the same arm twice under `--condition loss5` and compare its *own* two copies' full
metric sets, because a defect that makes two identical copies disagree is a race, and a
race is found by its timing, not by its averages.

**And the five-arm record itself is unusable, for a reason that is not the product
(2026-11-02).** The sweep finished and the gate on the full record reports **69
failures**, which reads like a catastrophe until the summary lines are read:

```
capacity: molehill sustained 8 stream(s)
capacity: l3      sustained 0 stream(s)
capacity: frp     sustained 0 stream(s)
coverage: nps / timeline / …  produced no measured round (all cells)
```

**Every arm failed, and the three peers have nothing to do with this carrier.** `l3`
lost `jitter` and `clean#2` as well as all eight capacity levels; `frp` sustained zero
streams; `nps` produced no measured round at all. A run in which the reference tools
cannot carry a single stream is a statement about the machine, not about `molehill`.

The leading explanation is a **blasted condition**. `_one_stage` installs a condition
per stage and never restores it; `run_staged`'s `finally` restores `ctx.condition`,
which is `None` for a staged run, so it restores nothing. The last stage of the
timeline is `clean#2`, whose condition *is* clean and therefore benign — but a stage
that dies early (as `loss5` did) leaves whatever it installed in place, and every
stage and every arm after it runs on that path. That would explain the whole shape:
one arm loses `loss5`, and four of its stages, two stages of the next arm and three
arms' capacity ramps follow it down.

**So the record is not committed.** A results file whose reference tools carried zero
streams cannot become `benches/records/results-bench-v1.0.0.json`, and nothing about
`molehill` should be concluded from it. What it does establish is a harness defect with
a blast radius of one whole sweep: **a stage's condition must be restored in a `finally`
of its own**, not by a cleanup that only fires for single-condition runs. That lands
before any further sweep, because until it does, one bad stage costs every measurement
after it — which is exactly how this cycle's first sweep came to be read as a product
failure.

**And the re-run's own distribution says the steady state is now at parity with TCP
(2026-11-02).** The harness fix worked where it was aimed — the cascade dropped from
five stages to two, and `rate100`, `rate20` and `jitter` all pass now — but the run's
`clean` stage reads 1 133 ms and its `clean#2` reads 3.6 ms, so the per-stage
distributions are worth reading directly rather than through the summary line:

| stage | n | p50 | p90 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| clean | 682 | **137.9** | 532.2 | 1 133.1 |
| rtt100 | 248 | 423.6 | 756.0 | 1 298.7 |
| loss1 | 1 396 | 42.5 | 274.5 | 1 104.9 |
| loss5 | 208 | 402.7 | 1 407.3 | 3 709.3 |
| rate100 | 1 236 | 122.3 | 179.0 | 188.3 |
| rate20 | 1 074 | 167.5 | 186.7 | 191.8 |
| jitter | 1 907 | 81.5 | 97.5 | 110.7 |
| **clean#2** | **2 604** | **2.2** | **2.6** | **3.6** |

**`clean#2` is the best arrival measurement this cycle has produced by a wide margin:
p50 2.2 ms, p90 2.6, p99 3.6 — better than TCP's own 2.24 / 2.59 on the same cell.**
It is also the *last* stage of the run, and the *first* stage of the same run reads
p50 137.9. Two stages with the same condition, the same binary, twenty minutes apart,
differing by sixty times at the median.

That is a warm-up effect, and it means **the gate's SLO failures are being produced by
the first stage of a timeline, not by a steady-state defect**. `clean#2` is reported
FAILED only because its *bulk* sample died with the same `control socket has closed`
that `loss5` shows — its arrival series is healthy throughout, 2 604 pings at p99
3.6 ms.

So three statements are now each true and must not be confused:

1. **Steady state is at parity with TCP** — 2.2 ms p50, 3.6 ms p99 against 2.24 / 2.59.
2. **The first stage of a run is slow** — 137.9 ms p50, and since the gate SLOs the
   clean stages it is what fails, not the steady state.
3. **Bulk samples fail intermittently** with `control socket has closed`, in `loss5`
   and in `clean#2` — a different defect again, and the one that costs coverage.

The next measurement is therefore about (2) alone: what makes the tool slow for the
first two minutes after it starts, when twenty minutes later it is at parity. Everything
else in the release picture is either measured good or already attributed.

**And the degraded mode is not the pool and not the opening — it is invisible at the
level a release run captures (2026-11-02).** That run's own artefacts, in the stage that
read p50 137.9 ms:

- **one `pool-stats` line, `established=4`**, and no `repaired` or `reaped` at all — the
  four lanes were healthy for the whole run;
- **zero `slow stream opening on the server` lines** — and that line fires at 100 ms, so
  if *half* the arrivals were taking 137 ms, many should have tripped it.

So the wait is neither the pool nor the stream open. It is before the open (the visitor's
accept→pairing wait) or after it (the first byte to the visitor's socket), and **both of
those are `DEBUG`** — `pairing budget expired` and the client's own slow-open line —
which a release run does not capture.

Two things follow. First, a correction to the paragraph above: across three runs the
first-to-last `clean` ratio is **1.0, 1.8 and 315**, so this is **not** a warm-up trend —
it is a *bimodal state*, and a stage lands in the good mode (p50 ~2 ms) or the degraded
one (p50 100+ ms) without a systematic reason visible in the artefacts a release run
keeps. Second, the next diagnostic run must be a **timeline with the crate at `DEBUG`**,
which is a dev-profile thing and not a release record: the release record keeps the
default filter, and the diagnosis is made beside it. That is the shape §10 asks for —
an instrument parameter is part of the method, so the two runs are not the same run.

Until that diagnostic lands, the release picture is: **steady state at parity with TCP,
`capacity_streams` 8 of 8, coverage mostly green — and a bimodal latency state whose
trigger is not visible in the record the release publishes.** That is what the gate's two
SLO failures are, and it is why the release is held rather than explained.

**And the diagnostic timeline names the wait: the pairing, fed by a handshake that
takes up to 613 ms (2026-11-02).** A `--scale 1.0` timeline with the whole crate at
`DEBUG` — the run the paragraph above asks for — read `clean: 713.1 ms … clean#2:
6.063 ms`, the same first-stage-bad, last-stage-good shape a third time. Its logs:

- **845 `visitor waited for its data channels` lines**, with `paired_us` up to
  **2 043 204** — visitors waited up to two seconds for a channel.
- **312 slow channel opens on the client**, with `us` = `hs_us` up to **613 889** and
  **`ack_us=0`** — the handshake, and the acknowledgement instant.

So the chain is: the visitor waits for a channel → the server asks → the client opens
one → **the client's Noise handshake takes up to 613 ms** → the pairing completes late.
And 613 ms is not a path latency: this carrier's round trip on that leg is sub-millisecond
and the one-flight open already made the exchange a single flight.

That puts the handshake's *packet* back in the frame, and it is the same question the age
bound was built for: the handshake is a stream's first bytes, so it is a data packet, so
the write path's age bound can refuse it while a bulk flight keeps the lane behind. **The
opening exemption was built and reverted two rounds ago — and the revert may have been a
mistake**, because the comparison it rested on was against a baseline run that was itself
in the degraded mode (`--condition loss5` gave 2.63 ms p50 with a 760 ms p99, which cannot
both be a 200 ms shaped path; with the exemption the same cell read 202 ms p50 and its A/A
twin agreed to the hundredth of a millisecond, which is what a 100 ms one-way delay
*should* read). The throughput comparison was equally polluted: 6.36 against a twin's
11.22.

**So the next measurement is an interleaved A/B — the exemption against this tree, under
`--condition loss5` — not another single-arm run.** That is the only form that can tell a
real 4× regression from a twin that was itself in the bad mode, and it is the difference
between reverting a fix and shipping one.

**And the A/B settles it: the revert was wrong (2026-11-02, `a395044`).** Interleaved,
four rounds each, under `--condition loss5` (100 ms, 1 %), with the exemption as A, the
tree without it as B, and an A/A twin in the run:

| | p50 | p99 | `bulk-n` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** (exempt) | 202.05 ms | **861.7** | 1.68 Gbit/s |
| B (no exemption) | 202.06 ms | **1 426.9** | 1.71 |
| A/A twin | 202.05 ms | 861.5 | 1.45 |

**The medians are identical to a hundredth of a millisecond; the tail is 40 % better
with the exemption; and the twin confirms it.** Throughput is inside the cell's own
scatter (1.68 against 1.71, twin 1.45). So the exemption costs nothing and buys the
`loss5` tail.

Two lessons, both already written down and both earned again here. **A single-arm
comparison under a lossy condition is worthless in this cell** — the earlier revert was
made against a baseline whose own A/A disagreement (6.36 against 11.22 Gbit/s) was
larger than the effect being judged. And **a median of 202 ms under a 100 ms one-way
delay is the correct reading, not a regression**: two traversals of the shaped leg. The
2.63 ms that a previous run showed at the same condition was the anomaly, and it is the
same degraded mode this whole round has been chasing.

So the release picture improves by one tail: the `loss5` stage's p99 with the exemption
is 861 ms, against 1 426 ms without. What it does not do is make `loss5` pass — and the
first-stage problem the diagnostic named (845 pairings waiting, a 613 ms handshake under
load) is a *different* effect that this fix only partly touches, because the handshake in
that measurement was slow on a **clean** path where the age bound was not refusing it.

**And it was not a different effect — the exemption fixed the clean path too
(2026-11-02).** That last sentence was wrong, and the next run says so. The same
`--scale 1.0` timeline on the tree with the exemption:

| | before the exemption | after |
|---|---|---|
| `clean` p99 | 713.1 ms | **56.87** |
| `loss5` p99 | 4 027.4 | **1 606.5** |
| slow pairings (≥100 ms) | **845** | **57** |
| worst pairing wait | 2 043 ms | **485 ms** |
| stages passing | 3 of 8 | **7 of 8** |

So the handshake *was* being refused by the bound on a path the bound was never meant
to police — a clean path under four bulk streams has a lane whose oldest data packet is
older than the RTO, which is precisely what the bound produces. **`845 → 57` slow
pairings and `713 → 56.9 ms` on the first stage** is the same defect that the `loss5` A/B
measured, seen from the other side.

Two things remain, and both are now small and named:

1. **`clean` is 56.87 ms against a 50 ms bar** — seven milliseconds, on 57 pairings of
   ~3 000 arrivals, with the worst at 485 ms.
2. **`clean#2`'s bulk sample ends at 120.02 s having been asked for 150 s.** The stage's
   hold *is* 150 s, so nothing in this loop cut it; the control socket closed 30 s early
   and the sample failed. That is the `control socket has closed` that has appeared in
   every run this cycle, and it is now the only thing standing between this tree and a
   green timeline. It is a probe-lifetime question, not a latency one.

Neither is the defect this cycle started with, and the gate's report should be read with
that in mind: the arrival path went from a p99 of 668 ms to 56.9 in the same run in which
the reference tools carried nothing.

**And the `control socket` cut is exactly 30 s, on the last stage only (2026-11-02).**
Three stages of one run, asked versus actual:

| stage | `-t` asked | wall |
|---|---|---|
| `clean` (first) | 150 s | 152.11 |
| `jitter` | 120 s | 122.42 |
| **`clean#2` (last)** | **150 s** | **120.02** |

The first two overshoot their own duration by the connect-and-omit overhead, which is
what a sample that finishes looks like. The last one is cut **30 seconds early** — and
120 is not a hold in the sweep timeline (`("clean", 150.0)` closes it), not a constant
in the carrier (`KEEPALIVE` 2 s, `DEAD_AFTER` 20 s, `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET` 5 s, `MAX_RTO`
30 s, `LOST_HOLD` 3 s), and not the iperf timeout (170 s). `stderr.txt` is empty and
`exit` is 1, so iperf3 reported the close rather than causing it.

The tool's own logs say nothing at that moment: the only `INFO` line in either process
after startup is a control-session retry at 14:57:19, which is *before* the stages. So
whatever closes the visitor's control connection at 120 s leaves no trace at the level
the run captures — **the same blind spot this round already paid for once on the pairing
line.**

Two candidates and both are cheap to separate: something in the harness holds a
120-second budget for the *last* stage (§10 says the client timeout must scale with the
test length, and 120 is a suspiciously round number next to a 150-second hold), or the
tool closes a stream it considers idle. The discriminator is one `INFO` line on the
tool's stream teardown path, which is a two-line change and the next thing to write —
because until it exists, every run reports "control socket has closed" with no side of
the connection named.

**And the instrument answers both questions at once (2026-11-02).** The next timeline on
the tree with it — a run that landed in the degraded mode, `clean: 800.97 ms` — produced:

- **923 slow pairings**, worst **1 486 ms**, against **57** and 485 ms in the good run
  two rounds earlier. So **the pairing is the discriminator between the two modes**, and
  the bimodality this file has been circling for ten rounds lives in one place: a
  visitor's wait for its data channel.
- **Every long-lived group ends with `lived_s` equal to its stage's length** — 152 for
  the first stage, then 122, 128, 130 for the ones after it, in five groups of four (the
  bulk streams), one group per stage. **The tool names its own end and never ends one
  early.**

So the 30-second cut is *not* the carrier: the group that carried `clean#2`'s bulk lived
**120 s** while the same stage definition one run earlier produced **152 s**, and the
stage is defined as 150. The tool reports the duration it actually lived, which means the
stage was cut at 120 — by whatever ends the *last* stage of a sweep early, not by anything
that closed a connection.

That is a harness question and it is now a narrow one: the last stage of the sweep dies
30 s short, the group's own `lived_s` proves it, and the carrier never closed a stream.
The pairing number is the other half: **57 slow pairings is a passing run and 923 is a
failing one**, on the same binary in the same afternoon, so the next investigation is what
puts the pairing path into the slow mode — and unlike everything before it, that question
now has a single instrument and a binary outcome.

**And the cheap reproduction gives the first-stage mechanism and a new anomaly
(2026-11-02).** `--scale 0.2` (7 minutes) reproduces both: `clean: 79.411 ms` against
`clean#2: 3.325`, with 27 slow pairings and all eight stages passing. Reading the
sender's window across that run, the four pool lanes:

| lane | first sample | mid | last |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 048 K | 4 709 K | 4 709 K |
| 1 | **100 K** | 4 188 K | 4 246 K |
| 2 | **13 K** | 3 725 K | 3 725 K |
| 3 | 2 048 K | 4 232 K | 4 232 K |

**The congestion window is cold at the start and takes the run to grow.** A lane opens
somewhere between its 13 KB initial value and the 2 MiB slow-start ceiling and reaches
~4.2 MB only later, so for the whole first stage the carrier is running a window eight
times smaller than the one it will settle on — and a small window on a lane carrying
four bulk streams is a queue that an arrival must wait behind. That is the first-stage
slowness, and it is exactly what `P2′` (pre-warmed authenticated channels) was reaching
for, one layer down: what needs warming is not the channel but the **window**.

And an anomaly that is not explained: **the server reports 33 distinct lanes while the
client's pool established 4 and repaired none** (`pool-stats` prints exactly one line,
`established=4`). The 29 extra ids each have nine window samples and a permanent 13 KB —
short-lived connections that opened, carried a little, and ended. Nothing in the client's
pool accounts for them, and `[client.data]` is empty in that arm's config, so `tunnels`
is the default four. Either something mints 29 short-lived carrier connections beside the
pool, or the server is counting something else as a lane; the next run should name them
(a lane that ends within a second has no business existing in a pooled design).

**And named from both ends, the anomaly sharpens: client 4, server 33 (2026-11-02).**
Counting distinct `lane=` ids in each process's own log for the same run:

| side | distinct lanes | which |
|---|---|---|
| client | **4** | ids 0-3 only |
| server | **33** | ids 0-3, plus 29 in the billions |

So it is **not** a client-side pool that grew: the client's pump has exactly the four
pool lanes and logs nothing else. The 29 are server-side `Conn`s created by the
listener for packet ids the client's pool never used as a lane. Two facts narrow it
and neither closes it:

- `data_enable = true` in that arm, so every visitor channel **is** carrying a Noise
  handshake — the per-stream-handshake premise this whole cycle has reasoned from holds;
- the client's `pool-stats` prints exactly one line, `established=4`, with no repair and
  no reap, so its pool never dialled a replacement.

What is left is that something on the client side mints a short-lived carrier
connection **beside** the pool — one the pool does not count, which is why no repair is
logged — and that is the shape of a *direct* data channel rather than a pooled stream.
The discriminator is already in the code and needs only the right log level: the server
routes a pooled stream through `mhd tunnel stream routed` and a direct one through
`do_v4_data_channel`'s `Handshaking a data channel`, and `core::server` was not at
`DEBUG` in this run. **One run with that module at `DEBUG` names them**, and if they are
direct channels then every arrival is paying a full connection rather than a stream on a
warm lane — which would be the largest arrival cost found in this cycle and the thing
`P2′` was really about.

**And the answer is neither pooled nor direct: every stream is pooled, and the 29 lanes
are strangers (2026-11-02).** The run with `core::server` at `DEBUG`:

```
direct (Handshaking a data channel):  0
pooled (mhd tunnel stream routed): 7 200
```

**Every one of the 7 200 streams took the pool** — so the pooled design is doing what it
says, the per-stream Noise handshake is real and on the arrival path, and the 29 extra
`Conn`s are not direct data channels. Their ids give them away: `3824123932`,
`3959218201`, `3959422976` are scattered across the whole `u32` range, while
`next_tunnel_id()` is sequential and the pool's four are `0..3`.

**A sequential minter cannot produce those numbers, so nothing in the client minted
them.** The listener's rule is "a decodable packet whose id it has never seen starts a
connection" — and the wire format carries no binding before the handshake — so **any
datagram that happens to decode as a packet creates a lane**: a `Shared`, a `Conn`, a
sender task and a 13 KB window, admitted without authentication and only bounded by
`MAX_CONNECTIONS` (4 096).

That is a robustness defect first and a measurement defect second. Robustness: an
unauthenticated peer can make the server allocate a connection per datagram, which is a
free amplifier and is exactly the class of thing `[server.data].max_tunnels` exists to
stop — except that valve counts *reserved tunnel slots*, and these never get that far.
Measurement: those strangers are counted as lanes in every per-lane instrument, which is
why a per-lane reading on the server has 33 rows where the client has 4.

The next change is small and both halves matter: a lane the server cannot attribute to a
session should be admitted only once its first stream proves a hello, or be counted and
rate-limited like a connection attempt. Until then, `lane=` on the server is not a lane,
and the per-lane numbers in this file that came from a server log have to be read with
that in mind.

**And warming the window faster makes the first stage worse, not better
(2026-11-02).** The cold-window reading above pointed at an obvious lever:
`INITIAL_CWND` is ten packets (13 KB), so a lane opens small and grows; starting it at
32 packets would let it reach its working size sooner. Built and measured at
`--scale 0.2`, one run each:

| | `INITIAL_CWND = 10` | `= 32` |
|---|---|---|
| `clean` p99 | 79.4 ms | **153.9** |
| `clean#2` p99 | 3.33 | 4.37 |
| `loss5` p99 | 2 467 | **1 440** |

**The first stage doubles.** So the window's *size* early on is not what makes the first
stage slow — a bigger initial window only gives the bulk streams a bigger burst to put in
front of the arrivals. Reverted.

That is the fourth lever this cycle has measured against the first stage and the third
that moved it the wrong way, and the pattern is now clear enough to state: **every change
that gives the bulk flight more room makes arrivals worse, and every change that gives it
less makes bulk worse.** The first stage is the two workloads competing, and no single
constant resolves that — which is what the `loss5` A/B and the `capacity` results have
been saying from different directions all along.

Two things are left for the remaining rounds and neither is a constant: the 29 strangers
(a robustness hardening, bounded today by `MAX_CONNECTIONS`), and the release measurement
itself — which needs a run in the good mode and now has an `INFO` instrument that says
which mode a run is in before its numbers are believed.

**The strangers are fixed, and the fix is proved by a test rather than by a run
(2026-11-02, `b6a71e0`).** The listener now creates a lane only for a datagram that
*opens a stream* — a `Frame::Stream` at offset zero carrying bytes, which is what a real
client's first datagram is (the selector byte) and what a stray is not. Everything else
is dropped before anything is allocated, so the `Shared`, the `Conn`, the sender task and
the window are never created for a stranger.

The negative case has its own test: `a_datagram_that_is_not_opening_a_stream_creates_no_lane`
sends a decodable packet with an unused id and `Frame::None` at a live listener and
asserts nothing is accepted. That is the evidence this round can offer, and it is the
right kind — the field count needs a `DEBUG` run to read `lane=`, and the run that
followed this change landed in the degraded mode (`clean: 510.8 ms`, 270 slow pairings)
with debug off, so it neither confirms nor denies anything.

Which is itself the useful observation: **the mode swings run to run on the same binary,
and two consecutive scale-0.2 runs read `clean` 153.9 and 510.8 ms.** Whatever produces
the mode is not the tree — the tree changed by one admission condition between them — and
it is the single largest variance in this cycle's measurements. Until it is understood, a
release measurement is a lottery, and the honest thing to publish is the distribution
rather than a run.

The remaining rounds go to two things in this order: name the mode with the instruments
that now exist (the pairing count says *which* run, the window says what it was doing),
and leave the tree with every gate green and the release held on a documented gap.

**And a correction that undoes an explanation this file has used for twenty rounds
(2026-11-02).** `churn-16`'s `params` read `"churn_per_s": 16` — the harness's rate is
**sixteen connections a second**, not sixteen at once. Each request is over in a couple
of milliseconds, so there is no concurrency in that cell at all, and every paragraph in
this file that attributed its tail to "sixteen concurrent arrivals contending for four
lanes" was explaining something that does not happen. The CHANGELOG and the benchmarks
page said the same thing in both languages and are corrected in `914e454`.

Two experiments fell out of the correction, and both are cheap because the cell is:

- **The tail is not the small-flight timer.** `MIN_RTO_SMALL_FLIGHT` is 20 ms and the
  p99 is 21 ms, which is the shape that has fooled this file six times. Set to 5 ms: p99
  **22.63** against an A/A twin's **22.26**, i.e. no improvement. Reverted.
- **It is not contention and not the lane count**, which the earlier 4/8/16 experiment
  already showed flat — and now that has a reason: there is nothing to contend.

So the honest statement of that cell is narrow and different from the one this file has
carried: at sixteen fresh connections a second on an idle path, about **one in a hundred**
requests takes 21 ms where TCP's worst hundredth takes 2.6, and the median is level. The
tail is a single-request cost that occasionally lands, not a queue — which is why every
lever aimed at queues (lanes, windows, pairings) moved nothing.

**And the tail is measurable once the instrument reads at the right scale: it is the
pairing (2026-11-02, `e7e5ba9`).** The pairing line's threshold was 100 ms — four times
the tail it was meant to catch — so it reported nothing, ever. At 5 ms, behind the same
stats switch as the opening line, one run of three rounds (6 400 requests a round):

| | pairings ≥ 5 ms |
|---|---|
| count | 5 035 |
| p50 | **8 084 µs** |
| p90 | 16 002 |
| p99 | 27 075 |
| max | 43 886 |

and the same run's `churn-16` reads p50 **2.45 ms**, p99 **20.47**. Those numbers fit
together exactly: a quarter of requests wait at least 5 ms for a channel, which leaves
the median untouched, and the worst of those waits are what the p99 catches.

**And the wait is not the open.** The client's own `mhd slow stream open` fires once in
that whole run, at the same 5 ms threshold. So a channel that takes 8-27 ms to arrive was
opened in under five: the time is between the server asking for a channel and that
channel's first packet arriving. Three things live there — the control channel carrying
the request, the client's pool handing the lane over, and the new stream's first datagram
reaching the server — and each is now one instrument away.

That is the first time this cell's tail has been localised to a stage rather than to a
suspicion, and it holds this cycle's lesson: **every threshold is part of the method, and
an instrument set four times too coarse reports a healthy system.**

**Read the paragraphs after this one before acting on it**: the sections below supersede

**Updated with the last two rounds' results (2026-11-02).** Three corrections since the
table above was written, and one new localisation:

- **`churn-16` is sixteen connections a second, not sixteen at once.** Every paragraph
  that read its tail as contention was wrong, in this file and on two user pages; all
  three are corrected.
- **The tail is the pairing, and its cost is the client's handshake.** Measured at last
  because all three instruments now read at five milliseconds behind the stats switch
  instead of at a hundred: a quarter of pairings take ≥5 ms (p50 8.1 ms, p90 16.0, p99
  27.1), the client's own open accounts for it, and **every microsecond of that open is
  `hs_us` with `ack_us` zero** — 291 slow opens in two rounds, p50 5.6 ms, worst 23.6.
  So one Noise handshake's round trip occasionally takes five milliseconds where the
  path's own is a tenth of one.
- **It is not a flush timer**: the pump's wait has no periodic flush (it selects on a
  notify, a closed signal and the connection's own timer), so a single write is flushed
  when it is made.
- **The guards cost nothing**: at four rounds each with an A/A twin, `churn-16` reads
  2.47 / 20.66 against 2.53 / 21.98 and `rr-16` 0.47 / 1.33 against 0.47 / 1.32. The

  cell produced earlier today, which is the host in its slow state rather than the
  change, and is the same variance that keeps the release held.

So the release picture is unchanged in substance and sharper in detail: **the steady
state is at parity with TCP, the capacity ramp reaches all eight levels, the multi-second
stalls are gone, and one Noise handshake in forty occasionally pays five milliseconds
instead of one-tenth** — which is what the two clean-stage SLO failures are, and what a
reviewer now has a number and a stage for.

**And three more candidates are excluded by measurement (2026-11-02).** Each was cheap
because `churn-16` is a two-minute cell:

| candidate | test | result |
|---|---|---|
| the small-flight floor (`MIN_RTO_SMALL_FLIGHT`, 20 ms) | 20 → 5 ms | p99 **22.6**, twin **22.3** — no change |
| the small-flight *initial* RTO (`SMALL_FLIGHT_INITIAL_RTO`, 20 ms) | 20 → 5 ms | p99 **22.1**, twin **20.3** — no change |
| worker starvation (`TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS`) | 4 against 16 | 20.4 / 22.3 against 21.6 / 18.3 — the twins' spread covers both |

Both timer constants were worth testing because 20 ms is the p99 to the millisecond and
this file has been fooled six times by a number that matched a constant. **Both are
refuted, and so is the scheduler-starvation story**: more workers change nothing, so the
wait is not the process competing for cores.

What is left is narrow and stated as such: one handshake in forty sees its two-datagram
exchange take ~6 ms (worst 23.6) where the path's own round trip is a tenth of one, on a
cell with no concurrency, no bulk, healthy lanes, a cold-free window and no timer
involved. That is **two userspace wakeups that occasionally cost milliseconds each**, and
the candidate space is now down to the reactor's wake path — the one place this cycle has
not instrumented, because the receive batch (`RecvBatch`, `recvmmsg`) has no timing on it
at all.

The remaining rounds go there or nowhere: `RecvBatch`'s wait-to-first-datagram is the
last stage in the chain without a number, and the honest alternative — if it is not
measurable in the time left — is to publish the distribution, which the CHANGELOG's Known
gaps already does.

**And the delay is one wake, seen by both ends (2026-11-02).** The two sides measure the
same exchange independently, and the numbers agree:

| side | what it measures | value |
|---|---|---|
| client | `hs_us`: opening message written → reply parsed | **5 639 µs** (p50 of 291) |
| server | `hs_us`: first read → handshake complete | **6 124** (its one slow line that run) |

The server's `hs_us` starts when it begins reading the stream's first bytes, so it
includes waiting for the client's opening message to arrive. Both ends therefore spend
about six milliseconds on the same exchange, which is what **one** delayed wake looks
like from either side — not a chain of small delays, and not a queue (there is no
concurrency in this cell to queue behind).

That is as far as this cycle can narrow it without a per-datagram timestamp on the wire,
and the honest statement is: **a single userspace wake on a loopback path occasionally
costs about six milliseconds, two and a half per cent of the time, and it lands on the
per-stream handshake because that is the only thing on this carrier's arrival path that
needs two of them.** A multiplexed carrier needs none per arrival, which is exactly the
structural difference the CHANGELOG's Known gaps describes — and it is now measured at
millisecond rather than second scale, with the queueing explanations all excluded.

**Eleven rounds remain and the work that is left is not another experiment.** The release
is held on two SLO failures whose numbers swing with a host state that has no instrument;
every mechanism reachable from the code has been measured; the tree is green and the
record is complete. The remaining rounds go to keeping it that way and to the end-of-session
ritual, not to a twelfth hypothesis.

**And the direction is systematic even though the magnitude is not — five runs, five

**And the `control socket` failure is at the *end* of a test, not during one
(2026-11-02).** That run's `jitter` sample was asked for 120 seconds and ran **120.38** —
a completed test — and still exited 1 with `control socket has closed unexpectedly`. Its
long-lived groups ended at `lived_s` 130-162, at or past the stage, so nothing closed a
data stream early either.

So the shape is: the data phase completes, and the *control* connection — a separate
forwarded stream that iperf3 keeps open across the whole test and uses to report — is
closed by the tool before the peer it is talking to has finished with it. That is a real
behaviour and a user-visible one: any protocol that finishes with a shutdown handshake
rather than a bare close sees a reset where it expected an orderly end. It is also the one
thing that has cost a cell of coverage in *every* run this cycle, which is why the gate has
reported missing cells more often than failing ones.

Converting that from "unknown" to "at end-of-test, on the control leg" is the last
narrowing this cycle can make. The fix — half-close and wait, rather than drop — touches
the close path for every visitor and needs its own measurement round, which is more than
the five rounds left can do honestly.

**And the forward idle watchdog is not it either** (`FORWARD_IDLE_TIMEOUT`, 300 s): a
control connection idle for a 120-second test never reaches it, and a group is only ended
when *both* directions have been silent that long. So the close happens at end-of-test
while the group is still alive by its own clock, which is why `lived_s` reported a
lifetime matching the stage rather than a truncated one.

Four rounds remain. The last thing this cycle does is leave the record in a state where
the next one can start: the tree green, every finding with its numbers, the release held
on two named SLO failures (one of them, in a good window, the cold start alone), and the
`control socket` narrowed to end-of-test on the control leg with four candidate mechanisms
excluded — the stage boundary, the group lifetime, the carrier's own close, and now the
idle watchdog.

**And a correction to the paragraph above: the tool did not close it either
(2026-11-02).** The arithmetic is against the earlier reading. That `jitter` sample's
control connection reports failure at **120.38 s**, and the group carrying it ended at
`lived_s` **130** — so the group **outlived the client's own exit by ten seconds**. A
connection the tool had closed cannot be reported closed by a client that has already
stopped, and a group still alive ten seconds later is the tool *holding* it open.

So the honest state of that failure is: **at end-of-test the client reports its control
socket closed while the tool is still holding the group open**, which puts the close on
the sink's side of the forwarded stream or in iperf3's own end-of-test handling, and not
on this carrier. That is the opposite of what the previous paragraph concluded, and it is
the fourth time this cycle a plausible reading of the same numbers has reversed on
arithmetic — which is why the arithmetic is in the record.

**The release gate's missing cells are therefore a harness-side open question, not a
carrier defect**, and the one thing the gate reports against this carrier remains the cold
first stage: 179.9 ms against a 50 ms bar in a good window, 12.13 ms at the median against
the 1.87 the same run reaches at its end.

**And the cold start's mechanism is withdrawn too (2026-11-02, `e3ed8a6`).** Three pages
said the first stage is worse *because its congestion window is still ramping from ten
packets*. That is an explanation this release has not measured, and the measurement it
would need contradicts it: the window reaches its 2 MiB slow-start ceiling within the
first second of traffic (the samples are one second apart and the first already reads
between 13 KB and 2 048 KB), so it cannot account for a median that stays **six times
worse across a whole 150-second stage**.

The pages now say what is true: the six-fold difference is the measurement, the mechanism
is unattributed, and the window is recorded as a **rejected** explanation so that the next
cycle does not spend its first round on it. That is the seventh time this cycle has had to
separate a number from the story told about it, and it is the same discipline that caught
the 41.3 ms turnaround, the "6.4 s RTO ladder", the 23 % four-process claim and the
`churn-16` concurrency — a claim must be a measurement, not a mechanism that would explain
one.



















3. **The tail follows the *shape*, not the tool's health**: `clean` and `clean#2` carry
   the multi-second maxima (4 157 and 3 223) with p50 1.9 and 1.1, while `rtt100` —
   the same clean path with 400 ms of delay — has a maximum of 506 ms. Delay
   compresses the tail; loss and jitter spread it.

**P3′'s gate, judged on these numbers.** `loss1`'s p99 is 1 076 ms, and the published
v0.11.2 record reads 1 083 ms for molehill, 1 065 for frp and 1 058 for rathole — so
at 1 % loss the p99 is an RTO for **every** tool in the record, a property of TCP's
retransmission under a drop shaper rather than of this carrier. A SACK-based fast
retransmit cannot improve it, for the structural reason already in this file: the
interactive flow has one packet in flight, and there is nothing behind a lost packet
to acknowledge past it. **So P3′'s stated gate is not reachable by P3′'s stated
mechanism**, and the honest action is to say so rather than to build it again — the
third item on the plan that the measurements have re-specified.



The capacity cell did improve sharply on the timer fix before the regression was
visible on other cells — p99 358, 821, 1 025, 1 715, 1 895, 2 061 ms against
2 100-5 000 before — so the mechanism is confirmed even though the change cannot
ship on its own.

**And the tail is not worker starvation — measured, three settings (2026-11-01).**
The process starts `min(cores, 4)` workers, so the obvious escape hatch is more.
`churn-16`, four rounds each, `TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS` set explicitly, mhd forced:

| workers | `rtt_p50_ms` | `rtt_p99_ms` | `rate_per_s` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 (the default) | **3.25** | **16.15** | **2 630** |
| 8 | 3.69 | 18.60 | 2 349 |
| 16 | 4.03 | 18.88 | 2 169 |

Monotone in the wrong direction on all three, so the tail is a fixed chain of
hand-offs rather than a starved runtime, and raising the worker count is not a
fix. (One round in each run collapsed to ~180 arrivals/s — the bimodality noted
earlier, still unexplained.) The numbers sit in `target/evidence/workers-*.json`.

**And the record layer is measured at three sizes: it buys the arrival tail at
every one of them and costs the bulk cell at every one of them (2026-11-01).**
Each row is the derived-key tree over the same baseline build (`--ab-arm`,
`--binary-b`, four rounds, mhd forced):

| record size | `churn-16` p99 | `churn-16` rate | `bulk-n` throughput | `bulk-n` samples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (the shipped tree) | 15.1–21.5 ms | 2 581–3 328/s | **12.29–12.32** | **5 of 5** |
| 32 KiB | −74 % (3.79 ms) | +100 % | −19 % (9.96) | 2 of 5 |
| 16 KiB | −78 % | — | 9.96 | 2 of 5 |
| **1 348 B (one packet)** | **−72 % (4.21 ms)** | **+146 %** | **−53 % (5.75)** | 4 of 8 |
| 1 348 B + per-stream credit | −72 % (4.21 ms) | +146 % | −53 % (5.75) | 4 of 8 |

So the two effects are both structural properties of "put an AEAD record layer
between the application and the carrier", and the record size only trades one
against the other: a bigger record costs less throughput (fewer AEAD calls) and
a smaller one fails less often (a shorter partial-record window), and neither
direction reaches both goals. **The record layer is the wrong mechanism**, and
this is the third granularity at which that has been measured.

**A fifth thing was tried and it is also refuted: the per-stream credit.** The
connection-wide `send_credit` is only refreshed by a dedicated `Frame::Credit`
every `WINDOW / 4` of reader progress, while the peer's per-stream read frontier
rides *every* acknowledgement block for free (`Ack::prefix`, already consumed by
`SendBuf::advance_to` to free buffer). So `Conn::write`'s bound used a batched
number where a current one was available — which looked exactly like the
deadlock. Making the bound `base + WINDOW - written` for the stream being
written changed **nothing measurable** (identical row above), so the credit path
is not the bulk cell's failure either. Reverted; the finding is recorded because
the reasoning was sound and the measurement is what rules it out.

**What is left, in order of size:** the arrival tail is an await-count problem
(measured above), the record layer cannot fix it without costing bulk, and the
two mechanisms that reduce awaits without a record layer are session resumption
(one round trip instead of two, with a ticket the lane issues at establishment)
and collapsing the pairing path's hand-offs. Both are unattempted.

**P4′ is half done, and the half that is left is left on purpose (2026-11-01).**
The two frame classes nothing sent are gone: a datagram frame and a whole-IP-packet
frame were declared, acknowledged and dropped by the connection, and no sender in
this dialect ever produced one — a UDP service and a transparent claim both ride
reliable streams. The kinds are now `Ack`, `Stream`, `Credit` and `Reset`, the
decoder refuses anything else, and the reader's size constants and round-trip case
list went with them.

The other half — tightening the pairing patience — is **not** done, because no
measurement says it should be. `PAIR_WAIT_BUDGET` (5 s) × `PAIR_ATTEMPTS` (5) is a
25 s ceiling on one visitor's wait, and the number that matters is not the ceiling
but that a *legitimate* cold open can take most of one budget: the client's own
dial has a 15 s budget, and the first visitor after a registration waits for a
lane that does not exist yet. Shortening it without a cell that measures the cold
path would trade a rare long wait for a rare truncated visitor. It stays, with the
reason written here rather than a number changed to look tidy.

**And P3′ was built and measured out (2026-11-01).** The rule was the one TCP
cannot implement: a packet is declared lost the moment the peer's *per-stream
cumulative byte prefix* passes its range, instead of waiting for three later
packets to be acknowledged. It was unit-tested in two cases (the proof fires; a
prefix on one stream never judges another), then A/B'd against the same build
without it, under `loss1`, on `bulk-n` and `rr-16`, four rounds with `--ab-arm`
and `--binary-b`:

- `rtt_p99_ms`: the run's floor is **0.10 %**, and the difference is inside it —
  no repair-latency effect at all;
- `bulk-n` `throughput_gbps`: floor 2.3 %, no difference;
- `retrans_segments`: **−1 464** directional for the rule, and *fragile* — one
  round's removal flips it.

Reverted, because a change with no measured win is one to drop rather than keep to
look tidy. The mechanism is sound and the reason it does not pay here is worth
recording: the request/response cells have **no bytes after a lost packet on the
same stream**, so the prefix can prove nothing and the peer waits for the
retransmit either way; and `loss1` is a *drop-based* shaper, so the bulk cell's
throughput is not RTO-limited and a faster repair has nothing to buy.

The A/A reading also needs one correction to an earlier entry: a twin that
reproduces a tail is evidence that the tail is *reproducible*, not that the cell
cannot resolve a change. What the twin cannot do is price a change by itself —
that is what `--ab-arm` with `--binary-b` is for.

- **Linux L3 takes the same device/address step macOS and Windows own
  (2026-10-19).** A Linux transparent service now creates its persistent TUN
  device when one is missing and, on the client, assigns each claimed address
  that is not already on it — exactly what macOS already does on its own (the
  device and the claimed addresses) and what the Windows server does for its
  adapter. No config key gates it: an existing device is used as it is (create
  it first to choose its MTU), and an address already assigned is left alone,
  so a second claim or a restart does not bounce a live interface. Routes,
  policy routing and forwarding stay the operator's on all three, which is the
  symmetry the maintainer asked for. An earlier version automated the routing
  half too (mark, policy rules, sysctls, `accept_local`); it was proven in a
  three-namespace topology and then withdrawn by decision. Two facts survive
  it: recipe B needs `net.ipv4.conf.<tun>.accept_local=1` (the manual recipe
  now documents it), and a device the daemon creates appears at
  startup/registration, so per-device sysctls must come from
  `net.ipv4.conf.default.*` before the start and routes that name the device
  must be applied after it appears — the ordering macOS and Windows recipes
  already have. The narrowed mode was re-proven on this host in the same
  topology, both recipes: the daemons created the devices and the client's
  address, the operator's steps followed, and the visitor was echoed through
  the claim. The default L3 harness ran again at `04f5c5d` on 2026-10-19:
  13/15 on the first run (the lending arms stalled) and 15/15 on a second; the
  device/address arms passed on both. A local variant that skipped the
  harness's own device setup created both
  devices and the client's address and passed every device-path arm, but its
  two lane-lending arms failed: the 16-flow arm stalled for about five seconds
  when a lane was lent, a window the default load finishes before. That is a
  lane-allocator observation, not root-caused here and not part of the device
  step.
- **Striped-group release and the striping signal were corrected (2026-10-19).**
  Two defects from the migration's striping commit. A group that ended by
  aborting a direction left its reader tasks parked on the mux streams, so the
  client's stream leases never came back — the saturated-pool test only passed
  because it restarted the client — and the target grew off *gather* latency, a
  proxy on the pairing path rather than path backpressure. The readers are now
  owned by the receive direction and aborted with it; the server releases an
  abandoned group on the client (`ReleaseStripedGroup`, tag 8 of the still
  unreleased v5.2 dialect, so it is extended in place); the client tombstones a
  released group so a stripe still in flight is dropped; and growth follows a
  group's own parked send direction (at least 250 ms, one step per 500 ms,
  capped at `MAX_STRIPES` 64). `a_saturated_pool_still_serves_the_next_visitor`
  now asserts the pool gets its streams back within 15 s and no longer restarts
  the client. No throughput claim is made from this: the sweep has to measure
  it, and it re-baselines anyway.

- **An L3 claim's lane budget is a live tuning surface, and its default is
  two.** The throughput ceiling is a serialized per-packet path, so a claim's
  throughput follows its lanes; four lanes buys 121 % of bulk throughput and
  costs the interactive stream its SLO headroom, so the default is the largest
  value that keeps both. The measurement, the cost in connections and the
  upgrade path are owned by [`DEFAULT_CLAIM_LANES`](src/common/constants.rs)
  and the configuration page; the full record — including the first version of
  that constant, which chose four from the bulk-only table — is in the archive.
- **Lending is the one mechanism this leaves unmeasured.** `lend` is on by
  default and moves an *idle* lane to the claim with more flows than lanes, and
  the new default now gives it slack to move. Its own benefit is still
  unestablished: the 7-second `bulk-n` cell cannot show it (lending needs ticks
  and confirmations, and each `dev` round restarts the processes), and the one
  run that did show it converging was voided by the shaper bug recorded in the
  archive. A long-hold scenario is what would settle it; the arms already exist

  The v0.11.1 tag was re-created on `4874f05` after a transient 0.11.2 bump was

- **Only docs and assets may follow a sweep.** `githooks/pre-tag` reads the
  results file's recorded revision and fails the tag if `src/`, `tests/`,
  `Cargo.*`, `build.rs` or the bench model's own code changed since — the
  changelog date and the README numbers may, code may not (AGENTS.md §10,
  "prove provenance").

  `release.yml` builds every artifact and runs `--help` on the native ones

## Open threads for the next cycle

- **Decision (2026-10-19): one top-level tunnel pool in both modes; the
  per-service/per-claim model is rejected, not renamed.** There is exactly one
  tunnel pool per control session (one per data endpoint), and every service
  draws its channels from it; `[client.services.<name>].tunnels` is removed.
  The same shape holds for L3: `[transparent.data].tunnels` is the client's one
  carrier-connection budget, and `[transparent.claims.*].tunnels` is removed —
  that key is a dead field today (the parser accepts it, the lowering never
  reads it; verified 2026-10-19 with a budget of 4 and two claims writing 8 and
  6: the client started and ran on 2 lanes each). The current per-service
  implementation is wrong; 0.11.2 replaces it with the model below.
  - **Defaults are the measured optima, not the cheapest value.**
    - **L4: `tunnels = 4`** — the shipped knee, and now the *total* width of
      one pool rather than four per service: yamux spreads streams over it (up
      to 56 per tunnel), and the 0.10 A/B found 8 does not move a mixed
      workload's throughput while costing 42-61 % of interactive p99 at 15+
      streams. One pool serves about 224 concurrent streams; a deployment
      above that raises the one key.
    - **L3: `tunnels = 2 × claims`** — the measured knee (1 lane 2.351 Gbit/s,
      2 lanes 3.283, 4 lanes 5.191 but p99 271 ms from three streams). Two per
      claim also leaves the spare lane `lend` needs: at one per claim the
      allocator can never lend, because a donor must have more than its last
      lane. The public `DEFAULT_CLAIM_LANES` goes; the derivation lives
      privately in the L3 module.
    - An explicit `tunnels` is always the **total**: L4 clamps to `1..=64`; L3
      must cover the claim count and is capped at 1024, with integer division
      leaving the remainder unallocated (write a multiple of the claim count).
  - `[client.data].shared_pool` stops being a switch: one pool is the only
    shape, so the key is removed (or kept as a no-op for one release — to be
    decided).
  - The proposed `default_tunnels` name no longer describes the key. With no
    per-service inheritance it is the pool's width, not a default; the final
    name is open (`tunnels` today).
  - The UDP-derived floor becomes the deepest demand across every UDP service
    that draws on the pool, and validation and runtime must read the same
    source; the first-service-width defect below disappears with the model.
  - Per-service `remote_addr` and `transport` still fragment the L4 pool today
    (the key is session + data endpoint, and the transport is the first
    service's), so the model needs a rule for them: refuse the override, or
    move both to the client-wide block. L3's per-claim `remote_addr` is fine —
    there is no shared pool, only a total count.
  - Pinned vs elastic stays open. "On-demand" today means channel placement on
    a pinned pool; the 0.10 elastic pool (grow on load, shrink on idle) was
    replaced in 0.11 for capacity predictability (CHANGELOG, "The tunnel pool
    is pinned"). If 0.11.2 also restores growth, that is a second decision.
  - The 0.10 measurement (shared p99 8.15 ms against per-service 5.00 at 19/20
    steps) is why the per-service default shipped. This decision overrides it,
    and the single-pool model needs its own measurement before any claim; `4`
    and `2 × claims` are the best-evidenced defaults until that sweep.
  Implemented in 0.11.2: `[client.data].tunnels` is the session's total
  width and `[transparent.data].tunnels` the L3 lane budget. This entry stays
  as the decision record.
- **Operator decision (2026-10-19): the production pair stays on forwarding
  (L4) until L3 is stable; L3 remains the target.** The maintainer's own
  deployment (ssh/http/https, Minecraft UDP, Mumble TCP+UDP) keeps the
  forwarding model for now and moves to claims when the gaps below close — the
  visitor's real source address is what a claim buys, and it is worth waiting
  for. The 0.11.1 client migration that decision needs is schema only:
  `default_mode`, `default_carrier`, `[client.data.tcp]`, `[client.data.kcp]`
  and the per-service `carrier` are gone, the carrier is chosen at runtime
  (KCP, TCP fallback), and a host that both forwards and claims runs two
  processes. No code change is implied by this decision.
- **Recipe B's single-IP client side is a documentation gap (found
  2026-10-19).** With the claim on the server's own public address, the client
  assigns that address to its TUN, so the kernel treats it as local and the
  client's control channel to `<server-ip>:2333` loops back to itself.
  `docs/deployment.md` says the client side is "recipe A's, unchanged"; that is
  not sufficient. Verified in a network namespace: demote the `local` table
  (`ip rule add pref 200 lookup local; ip rule del pref 0`) and add
  `ip rule add pref 100 iif lo to <server-ip> lookup main` — locally generated
  traffic then leaves via the gateway while inbound visitor packets are still
  delivered locally. Both language pages need the extra steps, and a single-IP
  acceptance case would keep it from regressing. A documentation and
  acceptance gap, not a data-path defect.
- **Naming decision pending: `[client.data].tunnels` vs `default_tunnels`
  (raised 2026-10-19).** The key is the client-wide default for every service
  that does not write its own `[client.services.<name>].tunnels`, which is
  exactly what `default_token`, `default_remote_addr` and
  `default_retry_interval` signal, so the unprefixed name reads as an
  inconsistency. It is `tunnels` today because the per-service key has the same
  name (the `default_` family is used where the child key is named
  differently), and because 0.10 deliberately replaced `default_count` with
  `tunnels` when the pool became pinned — the old "initial size" reading no
  longer applied. Options: a sentence in the configuration page naming it the
  default for services (cheap, preferred while the line is stabilizing), or a
  rename to `default_tunnels` through the removed-keys migration (parser
  refusal, the `githooks/check-docs` removed-key table, both language pages, an
  invalid-config test and an `[Unreleased]` entry). A rename leaves the
  per-service `tunnels` and `[transparent.data].tunnels` (a lane budget) alone.
  Superseded (2026-10-19) by the one-pool decision above: with no per-service
  inheritance the key is the pool's width, not a default, so `default_tunnels`
  no longer describes it. The final name is open.
- **`shared_pool`'s width is decided by whichever service activates first
  (verified 2026-10-19).** With `[client.data].shared_pool = true`, the session
  pool is created by the first service to become active and uses *that
  service's* `tunnels` (its override, else `[client.data].tunnels`), so a
  per-service override can size the shared pool. The comment on
  `ClientConfig::tunnels` says the client-wide count is the one a shared pool
  uses, and the config validation checks only that count against the UDP
  floor, so the runtime and the stated rule disagree. Reproduced with two
  services (`tunnels = 16` and `4`, client-wide `8`): four runs logged
  `tunnels=16` twice and `tunnels=4` twice, tracking activation order. Not a
  deployment issue for the pair above (it does not set `shared_pool`), but a
  defect to fix before the key's semantics are frozen: either honour the
  client-wide count in shared mode, or validate the per-service overrides and
  document the first-service rule. No fix made. Subsumed by the one-pool
  decision above (2026-10-19): the model removes the per-service pool and the
  switch, so the defect goes away with the replacement rather than with a local
  fix.
- **The 32-bit embedded targets are compile-checked, not test-run.**
  `5e585b7` closed the aarch64 half — the two full-set musl targets build in
  CI (x86_64 on `ubuntu-latest`, aarch64 natively on `ubuntu-24.04-arm`) and a
  native aarch64-musl test job runs the release's test command on every PR —
  and added a cross compile job for the three 32-bit `embedded` targets. A
  qemu test run for those remains the optional next step. The closure record
  is in the archive.
- **A config the product refuses was a config every check accepted
  (2026-10-13).** The mandatory-Noise rule lived in `run_instance`, so every
  parser-based check was blind: 24 documented examples, every bench arm's
  configs, both L3-acceptance ends and all three interop cases refused to start
  while `just check` stayed green. Two guards now exist (the doc-example test
  and `from_str`; `just bench selfcheck` loads each arm's config). **The general
  hole is open**: a rule enforced at runtime rather than parse time has no
  check that names it; start the next one in `from_str`.
- **Build times were decomposed (2026-10-13, 20 cores, rustc 1.99); the
  workspace split is measured and declined for now.** The inner loop is fast
  (check 1.3 s, clippy pass 1 9 s, the lib test binary 4.5 s); the felt
  slowness is the release build (71 s, user ≈ wall) under fat LTO. LTO-off is
  61 s and thin LTO 68 s, so fat LTO costs ~10 s; a split buys only finer
  check/test incrementality (1–4.5 s). Revisit when check times reach minutes
  or an architectural boundary needs enforcing; the dependency direction is
  already clean (`mux` ← `transport` ← `core` ← `main`, `mux` a
  zero-reverse-dep leaf). The benches-only classification now covers both hooks
  (`f9c0187`).
- **The safe-`nix` replacement for `udp_batch` is in.** The shipped variant
  rebuilds `MultiHeaders` per call (it is `!Send`), so the module has no
  `unsafe` left; a stored-header + `SmallVec` variant kept three `Send`/`Sync`
  proofs and measured the same. On the KCP `l4` path
  (`just bench --profile screen --arms l4 --ab-arm l4`, four runs) the
  raw-FFI baseline measured 1.566-1.578 s/Gbit against 1.590-1.602 for the nix
  variants: ~1.5-1.9 % higher CPU, consistently in the same direction. That is
  inside `cpu_s_per_gbit`'s 15 % materiality floor (no claim), so the safety
  win was accepted.
- **`quinn-udp` is not a drop-in replacement for this batching.** Its
  `poll_send` takes one `Transmit`, and GSO requires contiguous, equal-sized
  segments; KCP's batch is a mix of `Staged` and `Split` spans, so using it
  would mean copying every datagram or paying one syscall per datagram. Its
  `poll_recv` enables GRO, which returns coalesced datagrams that KCP would
  have to split by `stride` before its per-datagram accounting. That is a
  transport redesign with its own A/B, not a wrapper swap, and the `nix`
  wrapper already removed the local unsafe.
- **`tun-rs` is accepted for the cross-platform L3 cycle.** The earlier trial
  measured 1.1969 s/Gbit for the audited ioctl attach against 1.2045 for
  `tun-rs` (~0.6 % slower, inside the 15 % floor), and adds 29 crates and ~300
  lockfile lines; the cross-platform requirement is what changed the decision,
  not the cost. The three audited ioctls are gone, so production `unsafe` is
  now zero; `tun-rs`'s syscalls sit behind the dependency audit/deny gates.
  Vendoring only the used Linux subset was still rejected: 4,588 lines and 41
  `unsafe` blocks against the 299-line wrapper.
- **Protocol v5.1, and why it is a patch-release wire break.** The version is
  now `major.minor` (two bytes) and `StartForwardTransparent` carries the frame
  format (`Ip` or `Vnet`). A Linux pair negotiates `Vnet` and keeps the GSO
  fast path; any pair with a plain-IP device negotiates `Ip`, and the Linux
  side converts in `src/transparent/frame.rs`. v5.0 is refused on the
  connection it happens on. AGENTS.md §5 was updated: `5.1` is a dialect
  label, not a SemVer-compatible minor.
- **Both Linux L3 acceptance modes pass (2026-10-17).** `just l3-accept`
  (Vnet) and the same harness with `MOLEHILL_L3_WIRE=ip` (plain-IP wire) both
  returned PASS on every verdict, including transparency, no server-side
  flow state, bulk/MTU, 2,000 small round trips and 16 flows. The plain-IP
  run's bulk arm carried 314 packets at a mean 2,237 B/packet instead of 52
  super-frames at 7,614 B, which is the expected shape of the conversion
  path. The screen A/B for `tun-rs` on Linux has not been re-run since the
  cross-platform changes; it is deferred for v0.11.1 by the operator decision
  below, so this release makes no tun-rs A/B claim.
- **IPv6 is in v0.11.1, not deferred.** The v5.1 frame carries opaque IP
  packets, so this needed no wire bump: the work is the IPv6 parser (base
  header, common extension-chain walk with a header-count ceiling, fragment
  header, TCP/UDP ports, ICMPv6/ESP address-only, jumbograms rejected), the
  `gso_split` family argument, macOS `/128` assignment, Linux `ip -6`
  rules/routes and forwarding check, the Windows `/128` recipe, and tests.
  `just l3-accept-ipv6` passes on the `Vnet` wire and with
  `MOLEHILL_L3_WIRE=ip`: a visitor on an IPv6 path reaches a client-owned
  `/128`, the backend sees the visitor's IPv6 address, the server holds no
  socket, and a 60 KiB stream round-trips byte-exactly. The macOS/Windows
  IPv6 recipes still need real-host validation, like their IPv4 counterparts;
  that validation is deferred for v0.11.1 (see the deferral note below).
- **Windows L3 client is out of scope for v0.11.1.** Windows has no built-in
  source-address policy routing; a native client would need a WFP callout or
  WinDivert-class redirector, with a driver and its own security review. The
  config refuses it at parse time and names WSL2. macOS uses a pf
  `route-to` rule; the recipe still needs validation on a real Mac, and the
  exact syntax may depend on the utun's point-to-point peer. Windows **server**
  support is implemented (Wintun + `wintun.dll` + route/forwarding recipe) but
  also needs a real-host acceptance run; that run is deferred for v0.11.1 (see
  the deferral note below).
- **Deferred by operator decision for v0.11.1 (2026-10-18): macOS/Windows L3
  real-host acceptance, the `tun-rs` screen A/B and the lending measurement.**
  Linux `l3-accept` on both wire formats remains the only end-to-end L3
  evidence; the macOS pf/utun and Windows Wintun/routing recipes are documented
  but unvalidated on hardware. No tun-rs performance claim or lending claim is
  made from this release. These are accepted gaps, not blockers.
- **The five test-only env-mutation `unsafe` blocks can be wrapped, but the
  trade was declined.** `temp-env` 0.3.6 (`async_closure`) makes
  `set_var`/`remove_var` scoped and safe at the call site; a worktree
  conversion of the three multiplex tests and the pool handover test passed
  the full suites. It needs a dev-dependency (`futures` via `async_closure`)
  and re-resolves unrelated `windows-sys` entries in `Cargo.lock`, so it is
  not worth changing a sanctioned test-only waiver for it.
- **Privileged ports** are documented as *not* implemented (the whitelist admits
  any port it contains; the OS decides whether the bind succeeds). Enforcing
  `<1024` would be a behaviour decision for the human.
- **Carried over**: an HTTP API for configuration (hot reload is files-only),
  replacing the python bench project with `cargo-script` once it is stable,
  and QUIC (implemented and measured, parked in the `archive/transport-test`
  tag; revisit only for a UDP-only path or multi-stream loss isolation).
- **Repository settings are a human's to make**: branch protection for `main`
  and the release secrets. Nothing in this repository can enable them; they are
  the last release item outside the tree.
